title: Normal mechanical breath
نفَس آلي طبيعي
objective: Recognise a complete, normal breath on the pressure, flow and volume traces.
التعرف على نفَس آلي طبيعي ومكتمل على منحنيات الضغط والتدفق والحجم.
accessibleDescription: Pressure rises smoothly from the set PEEP of 5 cmH2O to a peak of about 25 cmH2O over one second, then drops back to 5 cmH2O and stays flat for the rest of the breath.
Inspiratory flow is constant at +30 L/min for one second. Expiratory flow is negative and returns to zero before the next breath begins.
Volume rises in a straight line from 0 to 500 mL during inspiration, then falls back to 0 mL during expiration, reaching zero before the next breath starts.

question.prompt: What does this set of waveforms show?
options: A normal breath, with exhalation completing before the next breath starts
Flow starvation from patient effort exceeding the set flow
question.explanation: The expiratory flow trace returns all the way to zero, and volume returns to zero, before the next inspiration begins - exhalation is complete. The pressure trace returns cleanly to the set PEEP and stays flat, with no residual elevation. There is no scooping or asynchrony in the pressure trace during inspiration.

evidenceSources: Goodfellow et al. AARC Clinical Practice Guideline: Patient-Ventilator Assessment (2024), PICO 1. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11298231/

title: Auto-PEEP (incomplete exhalation)
الضغط الإيجابي الذاتي (زفير غير مكتمل)
objective: Identify incomplete exhalation (auto-PEEP / dynamic hyperinflation) on the flow trace.
تحديد الزفير غير المكتمل (الضغط الإيجابي الذاتي) على منحنى التدفق.
accessibleDescription: The displayed airway pressure drops toward the set PEEP of 5 cmH2O during expiration. This trace does not show alveolar pressure.
Inspiratory flow is +37.5 L/min for 0.8 seconds. Expiratory flow remains negative when the next inspiration begins.
About 80 mL of the 500 mL delivered in the illustrated breath remains above the starting volume when the next breath begins.

question.prompt: What does this set of waveforms show?
options: A normal breath, with exhalation completing before the next breath starts
Flow starvation from patient effort exceeding the set flow
question.explanation: Persistent expiratory flow at the start of the next breath suggests incomplete exhalation and possible intrinsic PEEP. The volume trace shows retained volume above the breath's starting level. Intrinsic PEEP is estimated from total PEEP minus set PEEP using an end-expiratory hold under suitable passive conditions.

evidenceSources: Goodfellow et al. AARC Clinical Practice Guideline: Patient-Ventilator Assessment (2024), PICO 1. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11298231/

title: Flow starvation
نقص التدفق
objective: Identify flow starvation (a scooped pressure trace) during a volume-controlled breath.
تحديد نقص التدفق (منحنى ضغط متقعّر) أثناء نفَس محدد الحجم.
accessibleDescription: Pressure rises at the start of inspiration, dips to about 8 cmH2O halfway through inspiration, then rises again near the end.
Inspiratory flow is constant at +30 L/min for one second. Expiratory flow is negative and returns to zero before the next breath begins.
In this example, the fixed flow delivers 500 mL. On a real ventilator, a pressure limit, leak or interrupted breath can reduce delivered volume.

question.prompt: What does this set of waveforms show?
options: A normal breath, with exhalation completing before the next breath starts
Flow starvation from patient effort exceeding the set flow
question.explanation: With fixed inspiratory flow, a dip in airway pressure can reflect active inspiratory effort when delivered flow falls short of the patient's demand. Assess the patient alongside the waveform. Expiratory flow reaches zero before the next breath in this example.

evidenceSources: Goodfellow et al. AARC Clinical Practice Guideline: Patient-Ventilator Assessment (2024), PICO 1. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11298231/
Optimizing Mechanical Ventilation: Identification and Management of Patient–Ventilator Asynchronies (2024), Flow Starvation. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11721790/
